{{short description|American physicist, mathematician, and computer scientist}}

'''E. Mark Gold''' (often written "E Mark Gold" without a dot,<ref name="Gold.1966"/><ref name="Gold.1967"/><ref name="Gold.1971"/><ref name="Gold.1973a"/><ref name="Gold.1973b"/><ref name="Gold.1974"/><ref name="Gold.1978a"/><ref name="Gold.1991"/> born 1936 in [[Los Angeles]])<ref name="Gold.1965b">{{cite thesis | type=Ph.D. thesis | author=E. Mark Gold | title=Models of Goal-Seeking and Learning | institution=UCLA | series=UCLA dissertation, University Microfilms, Inc. | volume=65-6031 | date=Jan 1965 | id={{ProQuest|302181018}} }}</ref>{{rp|vi}} is an American physicist, mathematician, and computer scientist. 
He became well known for his article ''[[Language identification in the limit]]''<ref name="Gold.1964">{{cite report | url=https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_memoranda/RM4136.html | author=E. Mark Gold | title=Language identification in the limit | institution=RAND Corporation | type=RAND Research Memorandum RM-4136-PR | year=1964 }}</ref><ref name="Gold.1967">{{cite journal | author=E Mark Gold | title=Language Identification in the Limit | journal=Information and Control | volume=10 | number=5 | pages=447&ndash;474 | date=May 1967 | doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5 | doi-access=free }}</ref> which pioneered a formal model for [[inductive inference]] of [[formal languages]], mainly by computers.
Since 1999, an award of the conference on [[algorithmic learning theory]] is named after him.<ref>[https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~fstephan/alt/alt2017/id.html ''Important dates'']  page for ALT'17</ref><ref>[https://www-alg.ist.hokudai.ac.jp/~thomas/ALT13/gold.html E.M. Gold Award Winners 1999&ndash;2012] at ALT'13</ref>

==Academic education==
In 1956, he got a [[B.S.]] in mathematics from the [[California Institute of Technology]],
in 1958, he got a [[M.S.]] in physics from [[Princeton University]].<ref name="Gold.1965b"/>{{rp|vi}}
In Jan 1965, got his Ph.D. from [[UCLA]], supervised by [[Abraham Robinson]].<ref name="mathGenealogy">{{mathGenealogy|48836}}</ref><ref name="Gold.1965b"/>{{rp|i}}<ref>Also in the examination committee were John L. Barnes, [[Leo Breiman]], [[Jacob Marschak]], and Charles B. Tomkins; some of them might have been advisors.</ref><ref name="Gold.1971">{{cite journal | author=E Mark Gold | title=Universal goal-seekers | journal=Information and Control | volume=18 | number=5 | pages=395&ndash;403 | date=Jun 1971 | doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(71)90474-8 | doi-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|403}}

==Scientific career==
Gold's most influential contribution is the "Language Identification in the Limit" framework, often referred to as Gold's Theorem. This work established the mathematical foundations for how a computational system can learn a formal language from a sequence of examples. He demonstrated that while certain classes of languages (like regular languages) are identifiable in the limit, others, such as the class of all context-free languages, are not learnable from positive examples alone.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Gold |first=E. Mark |date=1967 |title=Language Identification in the Limit |journal=Information and Control |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=447–474 |doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(67)91165-5}}</ref> This discovery had a profound impact on [[computational linguistics]] and [[artificial intelligence]].
